name: Cutting red meat for smell
lead: Cutting red meat for smell is the practice of reducing red meat intake in the belief that it improves body odor, so that a person smells fresher and more pleasant to others up close. It is one of several diet-based approaches, alongside fruit and vegetable intake, that people in appearance communities discuss for being more attractive in presence as well as in looks.[1][2]

The main published study is a 2006 experiment in Chemical Senses by Havlicek and Lenochova. Seventeen male donors followed a meat diet and a non-meat diet for two weeks each, in counterbalanced order, wearing armpit pads for the last 24 hours of each diet. Thirty women not using hormonal contraceptives rated the samples; odor from the non-meat diet was rated as more attractive, more pleasant and less intense.[1] The authors concluded that red meat consumption negatively affects the perceived pleasantness of body odor.[1]

Body odor arises mostly when skin bacteria act on secretions from apocrine sweat glands, and Wikipedia notes that food, drink and the gut microbiome can influence it; one study it cites found that men who ate more fruit and vegetables had more pleasant-smelling sweat.[2][3]

angle.text: People cut red meat hoping their natural scent will read as more pleasant to others. The one controlled study found odor from a meat-free diet was rated more attractive and less intense.

infobox: Less intense, more pleasant body odor

paras: The practice means lowering or removing red meat in the hope of a more pleasant body scent. Axillary odor results mainly from bacteria such as Corynebacterium converting apocrine sweat secretions into odorous fatty acids and sulfur compounds, and genetics, notably the ABCC11 gene, also play a role.[2] Wikipedia states that diet and the gut microbiome can affect body odor, without naming red meat.[2]

In the 2006 Chemical Senses study, 17 men followed a meat and a non-meat diet for two weeks each in counterbalanced order, then repeated the procedure a month later with the opposite diet; axillary pad samples were rated by 30 women. Non-meat samples were rated as more attractive, more pleasant and less intense.[1] The study was small, and raters were women not using hormonal contraceptives.[1]
A separate study cited by Wikipedia found that men who ate more fruit and vegetables had sweat described as floral, fruity and sweet.[2]

For persistent or strong odor, Wikipedia lists antiperspirants containing aluminum chloride, deodorants, daily antibacterial washing and, for severe cases, surgery, alongside general dietary influences.[2]

timeline.event: Havlicek and Lenochova publish the meat versus non-meat diet body odor study in Chemical Senses.[1]

card.summary: A controlled study in men reportedly rated sweat from a meat diet as less pleasant; evidence is small.
card.note: Based on one reported small controlled study.

quick.overview:
Some people cut red meat hoping to smell better. A controlled study of men on meat or non-meat diets reportedly found the meat group's odor rated less pleasant and more intense.

The evidence summarized here rests mainly on that one study.
quick.mechanism: Diet is thought to change compounds excreted in sweat; specifics are not given in the sources consulted.
quick.risks: Nutritional effects of dietary changes were not covered in the sources consulted.
